title: Rectification of Errors
tagline: Classifying accounting errors, using the suspense account, and correcting mistakes before and after the final accounts.

overview.intro: Books are kept by people, and people make mistakes. An error of principle charges revenue against capital; an error of commission posts the right amount to the wrong person’s account; an entry is simply left out. This unit first classifies the errors, then shows how a suspense account isolates a difference so that the trial balance can still agree, and finally works through the two standard situations: errors discovered before the final accounts are prepared, and errors discovered afterwards, when the correction must be routed through the next year’s profit and loss account so that the earlier statements are not restated.

facts.label: Error classes
facts.value: Omission, commission, principle, original entry, compensating, complete reversal of entry.

facts.label: Suspense account
facts.value: Opened with the difference so the trial balance agrees; closed when every rupee of the difference is explained.

facts.label: After final accounts
facts.value: Personal and real account errors are corrected through the profit and loss adjustment account of the next period.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Rectification entries and suspense account questions appear in most yearly ISC papers.

learningOutcomes: Classify errors according to their nature and effect on the trial balance.
Explain the use of a suspense account and how it is cleared.
Rectify errors detected before the preparation of final accounts.
Rectify errors detected after the preparation of final accounts.
Explain why compensating and omission errors escape the trial balance.

blocks.text: Errors are grouped by how they arise, because the method of correction depends on the class. An error of omission leaves a transaction out entirely, either completely, when neither the debit nor the credit is recorded, or partially, when one side only is posted. An error of commission posts the correct amount to the wrong account of the same class, such as crediting Ram instead of Rahim. An error of principle treats a capital item as revenue, for example charging the purchase of a delivery van to repairs. An error of original entry copies the wrong figure from the source document into the journal, and every posting made from it inherits the mistake.

items.text: A bill receivable of ₹9,000 is not recorded at all.
items.note: A complete omission leaves the trial balance agreeing, which is why it is found only by reading the books or by a chance reference.

items.text: Repairs of ₹4,000 are posted to the machinery account.
items.note: An error of principle overstates the asset and understates the expense, yet the trial balance agrees.

blocks.text: When the trial balance disagrees, the difference is temporarily placed in a suspense account so that the books can be balanced and the final accounts prepared in time. The side that is short receives the difference: if the debit column totals ₹8,000 less than the credit column, suspense is debited with ₹8,000 in the trial balance. Each error discovered that affects the difference is then corrected through suspense, and the balance of suspense is extinguished exactly when every rupee of the difference has been located. A suspense account with a residual balance at the year end means an error is still at large.

items: Open suspense only when the trial balance fails to agree.
Post the difference to the shorter side so that the two columns agree.
Correct each one-sided error through suspense as it is found.
Clear the account completely; a closing balance means an unlocated error.
If the final accounts are prepared while suspense still stands, the balance is carried forward as a floating liability or asset.

items.text: Sales of ₹6,500 were posted as ₹5,600 in the ledger.
items.note: The account is short by ₹900 on one side, so suspense is debited with ₹900 and Sales credited with the missing amount.

items.text: Wages of ₹1,200 were credited instead of debited.
items.note: The error has moved ₹2,400 out of place, so suspense is debited with ₹2,400 to correct both the false credit and the missing debit.

learn.title: Rectification before the final accounts are prepared

blocks.text: Errors found while the books are still open are corrected by a counter-entry that reverses the effect of the mistake and puts the accounts right. The logic is simple: whatever the wrong entry did, the rectifying entry must undo. A wrong debit is cancelled by a credit and vice versa, and where an amount was posted to the wrong account, the amount is transferred from that account to the account that should have received it. Errors of principle are corrected by moving the amount out of the revenue account into the asset account, or the other way round.

blocks.caption: Rectification entries for errors found before final accounts
rows: Rent paid ₹3,000 posted to the debit of the proprietor’s personal account
Rent a/c Dr 3,000 to Proprietor’s personal a/c 3,000
Purchase of machinery ₹12,000 charged to purchases account
Machinery a/c Dr 12,000 to Purchases a/c 12,000
Sale of ₹4,200 entered as ₹2,400 in both books
Debtors a/c Dr 1,800 to Sales a/c 1,800
₹700 paid to Anil posted to Anand
Anand a/c Dr 700 to Anil a/c 700
Bill discounted ₹5,000 credited to bills receivable twice
Bills receivable a/c Dr 5,000 to Discount received a/c 5,000

blocks.text: When the error is one-sided, the suspense account is the counterparty, because only one side of the books is wrong and the difference has to be absorbed somewhere. When both sides of the entry are wrong but in equal measure, suspense is not involved at all, and the correction simply reverses the original pair of postings. In either case the rectifying entry is dated when the error is discovered and is posted to the ledger in the ordinary way.

learn.title: Rectification after the final accounts are prepared

blocks.text: Once the previous year’s statements have been prepared and published, the earlier figures are not reopened. Instead, the correction passes through the books of the current period using a profit and loss adjustment account, which is a nominal account representing the prior year’s profit and loss. A personal or real account error is corrected by transferring to this account: for instance, if machinery was wrongly charged to repairs in the closed year, the current entry debits machinery and credits profit and loss adjustment, thereby restoring the asset without disturbing this year’s trading result.

blocks.caption: Rectification after the year end
rows: Machinery charged to repairs
Machinery a/c Dr, to Profit and loss adjustment a/c
Purchases charged to machinery account
Profit and loss adjustment a/c Dr, to Machinery a/c
Depreciation undercharged in the closed year
Profit and loss adjustment a/c Dr, to Machinery a/c
Closing stock understated
Stock a/c Dr, to Profit and loss adjustment a/c

items.text: Repairs of ₹8,000 were wrongly debited to the machinery account in the closed year.
items.note: Current entry: Repairs a/c Dr 8,000 to Profit and loss adjustment a/c 8,000, restoring the expense to this year’s charge as a prior-period correction.

items.text: A creditor of ₹5,000 was omitted from the last balance sheet.
items.note: Current entry: Profit and loss adjustment a/c Dr 5,000 to Creditor’s a/c 5,000, bringing the liability into the accounts at the point of discovery.

blocks.text: A trial balance that agrees is not a certificate of accuracy. Detection therefore relies on layered checks. Recomputing totals and balances catches arithmetical slips; comparing the ledger with the source documents catches omission and original-entry errors; reading the ledger accounts for amounts that are obviously out of range catches errors of principle; and a scrutiny of the trial balance for accounts whose balances are unusual, such as a credit balance in an asset account, exposes misclassifications. Where a difference exists, locating it starts from the amount itself: halving the difference suggests a complete reversal of entry, while a difference that is a multiple of nine suggests a transposition of digits.

items: Halve the difference: if the half equals the difference, suspect a debit posted as credit.
Test divisibility by nine: transposed digits such as 54 for 45 leave a difference of nine.
Check that every subsidiary book total has been posted to the ledger.
Read the ledger for balances of the wrong nature, such as a creditor showing a debit.
Confirm that the total of the trial balance agrees with the sum of the ledger balances.

blocks.text: Errors of principle and compensating errors are the hardest to detect because nothing fails to add up, and they are found by reading the final statements with an accounting question in mind: does a delivery van really belong in repairs, and does this expense look too small for a business of this size?

keyPoints: Errors are classified as omission, commission, principle, original entry, compensating and complete reversal.
A complete omission and an error of commission leave the trial balance agreeing.
An error of principle charges a capital item to revenue or the reverse.
A suspense account absorbs the difference so that the books can be balanced.
Suspense is cleared completely once every rupee of the difference is explained.
Rectification before final accounts uses a counter-entry that reverses the mistake.
Rectification after final accounts passes through the profit and loss adjustment account.
Errors of personal and real accounts are corrected against profit and loss adjustment.
A halved difference suggests a complete reversal of entry.
A difference divisible by nine suggests transposed digits.
examFocus: Name the class of error before correcting it; the diagnosis usually carries as many marks as the entry.
State explicitly whether the error was found before or after final accounts, because the route of correction depends entirely on it.
Show the amount by which a transposed or misposted figure must be doubled when it affected only one side.

vocabulary.meaning: A transaction left out of the books completely or on one side only.
The correct amount posted to the wrong account of the same class.
Treating a capital item as revenue, or a revenue item as capital.
Two mistakes of equal value that cancel each other’s effect on the totals.
Temporary account used to hold the difference until the error is found.
Account used after the year end to route corrections of prior-year errors.
Mistake in which digits are written in the wrong order, such as 54 for 45.

questions.prompt: An error where the correct amount is posted to the wrong account of the same class is called:
questions.explanation: Posting a creditor’s amount to another creditor is an error of commission: the class is right and only the account is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which of these errors will leave the trial balance agreeing?
options: A transaction posted to only one side
The purchase of a van charged to repairs
An outstanding expense left unrecorded in the ledger entirely
questions.answer: The purchase of a van charged to repairs
questions.explanation: An error of principle keeps both sides equal because the amount was posted, just into the wrong class of account.

questions.prompt: The suspense account is used when:
options: The trial balance fails to agree
Final accounts have already been published
questions.answer: The trial balance fails to agree
questions.explanation: The difference is parked in suspense so that both columns agree and the books can still be balanced and closed.

questions.prompt: An error of ₹12,000 in a personal account is discovered after the final accounts have been prepared. It is corrected by:
options: Debiting the personal account and crediting the profit and loss adjustment account
Opening a suspense account in the current year
Adjusting the previous year’s published statements
Writing the amount off as a bad debt immediately
questions.answer: Debiting the personal account and crediting the profit and loss adjustment account
questions.explanation: The profit and loss adjustment account stands in for the closed year’s profit and loss account, so prior-year errors are corrected without restating published figures.

questions.prompt: Two mistakes of equal amount that cancel each other so that the trial balance still agrees are called __________ errors.
questions.explanation: Because the two mistakes are equal and opposite in effect, the totals remain equal and the errors are found only by inspection.

questions.prompt: A difference divisible by nine usually suggests an error of __________ , where digits are written in the wrong order.
questions.explanation: Swapping 54 for 45 changes the value by nine, so a difference of nine or a multiple of it points to reversed digits.

questions.prompt: Classify each of the following and state whether the trial balance will agree: (a) rent paid posted to the debit of the proprietor, (b) a sale of ₹800 recorded as ₹80, (c) cash received from a customer not recorded at all.
questions.answer: (a) An error of principle, and the trial balance still agrees because both sides carry the same total. (b) An error of original entry, and the trial balance agrees if the wrong figure entered both the debit and the credit. (c) A complete omission, and the trial balance agrees because neither side was recorded.
questions.explanation: Three classifications are needed, and the effect on the trial balance must be stated for each, since that is the point of the classification.

questions.prompt: What is a suspense account and when is it closed?
questions.answer: A suspense account is a temporary account in which the difference between the debit and credit totals of a trial balance is placed so that the books can be balanced and the final accounts prepared while an error is still being traced. It is debited or credited with the difference according to the shorter side, is reduced as each one-sided error is corrected, and is closed in full once every rupee of the difference has been explained.
questions.explanation: Both parts are required: how the account is opened and the condition on which it can be closed.

questions.prompt: A machinery purchase of ₹45,000 was charged to the repairs account in the year ended 31 March, and the error is found in the following June after the accounts were prepared. Pass the rectifying entry.
questions.answer: Since the final accounts of the closed year have already been prepared, the correction is passed through the profit and loss adjustment account. The entry in the current year is: Machinery a/c Dr 45,000 to Profit and loss adjustment a/c 45,000. The asset is restored in the balance sheet at its correct amount and the prior-year charge is corrected through the adjustment account, so the trading result of the current year is unaffected.
questions.explanation: The entry must name the profit and loss adjustment account rather than the current profit and loss account, and the reason that the closed year’s statements are not reopened must be stated for full marks.

questions.prompt: A trial balance shows the credit column exceeding the debit column by ₹2,400. Two one-sided errors are found: a debit of ₹1,600 was never posted at all, and a debit of ₹400 was posted to the credit side instead of the debit side. Show how suspense is opened and then cleared.
questions.answer: The credit column is heavier by ₹2,400, so the difference is debited to suspense in the trial balance, leaving suspense with a debit balance of ₹2,400. The first error leaves the debit side short by ₹1,600, so it is corrected by debiting the account that should have received it and crediting suspense with ₹1,600. The second error both fails to debit ₹400 and wrongly credits ₹400, a total displacement of ₹800, so that account is debited ₹800 and suspense is credited ₹800. Suspense is credited 1,600 + 800 = ₹2,400 in all and therefore stands nil.
questions.explanation: The question demands a direction check for each error: the missing debit is restored through suspense, while the misposted amount must be corrected twice over, and the two entries together must extinguish the suspense balance exactly.
